paragraphs.title: Returning to the Lord and Preparing the Heart

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “If thou wilt return, O Israel... return unto me.”
easy.q: To whom is Israel called to return?

easy.explanation: Israel was told to put away its abominations from the Lord’s sight.
easy.q: What was Israel to put away?

easy.explanation: They were commanded to circumcise themselves and take away the foreskins of their hearts.
easy.q: What were Judah and Jerusalem told to do to their hearts?

medium.explanation: The verse names truth, judgment, and righteousness.
medium.q: In what should the people swear, “The Lord liveth”?

answers: Breaking up fallow ground and removing thorns
medium.explanation: The Lord says, “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.”

answers: Do not sow before the rain
Do not plant in a foreign land
Do not seek goodness without first removing evil
medium.explanation: The image teaches that the heart must be prepared before good can grow.
medium.q: What does “sow not among thorns” mean in context?

answers: Turning truly to the Lord leads to blessing among the nations
Blessing comes only after building cities
challenge.explanation: Returning to the Lord in truth, judgment, and righteousness is connected with the nations blessing themselves in him.
challenge.q: How are putting away abominations and blessing the nations connected?

answers: The evil of the people’s doings
challenge.explanation: The Lord’s fury comes because of “the evil of your doings.”
challenge.q: What does the fire of the Lord’s fury warn against?

answers: The heart must be made strong for war
An inward barrier to repentance must be removed
challenge.explanation: The phrase pictures removing the inner obstacle that prevents cleansing and change.
challenge.q: What moral idea is expressed by “the foreskins of your heart”?

paragraphs.title: The War Alarm and the Enemy from the North

easy.explanation: The command was, “Blow ye the trumpet in the land.”
easy.q: What were the people told to blow?

easy.explanation: They were told, “Assemble yourselves, and let us go into the defenced cities.”
easy.q: Where were the people told to gather?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I will bring evil from the north.”
easy.q: From which direction would the evil come?

answers: To a lion coming up from his thicket
To a bird descending from heaven
To a farmer plowing a field
medium.explanation: The enemy is described as a lion coming up from his thicket.
medium.q: How is the enemy first compared?

answers: The fierce anger of the Lord was not turned back
medium.explanation: Their mourning was required because the Lord’s fierce anger had not turned back.
medium.q: Why were the people told to wear sackcloth, lament, and howl?

medium.explanation: The context describes desolation, wasted cities, and a great disaster.
medium.q: What does “destruction” mean in this passage?

challenge.explanation: The people are warned by trumpet, told to gather, and then told to retreat because destruction is coming.
challenge.q: Which sequence best describes the response to the danger?

answers: That the threat is fierce and not a gentle wind for winnowing
That the enemy remains in one place
challenge.explanation: The wind is described as a full, harsh wind, not one used to fan or cleanse grain.
challenge.q: What does the image of the desert wind emphasize?

answers: Every city is forsaken without an inhabitant
challenge.explanation: The cities are laid waste and left without inhabitants.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the judgment includes the abandonment of cities?

paragraphs.title: The Threat against Jerusalem and Its Responsibility

easy.explanation: Jerusalem is told, “Wash thine heart from wickedness.”
easy.q: To whom is the command to wash the heart addressed?

easy.explanation: A voice declares from Dan, and affliction is published from Mount Ephraim.
easy.q: From what places are warning voices heard?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Thy way and thy doings have procured these things unto thee.”
easy.q: What brought these things upon Jerusalem?

answers: That the city might become wealthy
That the walls might be enlarged
medium.explanation: Jerusalem is told to wash her heart “that thou mayest be saved.”
medium.q: What was the purpose of washing Jerusalem’s heart?

answers: It comes from the south and then from the sea
It is heard from Dan and Mount Ephraim and reaches Judah’s cities
It begins in Jerusalem and disappears
medium.explanation: The warnings come from the northern places, and watchers give out their voice against Judah’s cities.
medium.q: How does the warning advance through the passage?

answers: Forces watching or besieging the cities
medium.explanation: The watchers are military forces coming against and surrounding Jerusalem’s cities.
medium.q: What are “watchers” in this military context?

answers: Cleansing the heart from wickedness is presented as the way to be saved
Deliverance depends only on outward ornaments
There is no connection between conduct and consequences
challenge.explanation: Jerusalem is told to wash her heart from wickedness so that she may be saved.
challenge.q: What connection does the passage make between repentance and deliverance?

answers: The threat becomes immediate and approaches the cities
challenge.explanation: The warning progresses from voices in the north to forces stationed against Judah’s cities.
challenge.q: What does the movement from distant warnings to watchers against the cities show?

challenge.explanation: Jerusalem’s vain thoughts are empty, sinful thoughts that lodge within her.
challenge.q: What are “vain thoughts” in this context?

paragraphs.title: The Prophet’s Cry before the Destruction

answers: The sound of the trumpet and the alarm of war
easy.explanation: He hears the trumpet and the alarm of war.
The passage says, “Destruction upon destruction is cried.”
easy.q: What is cried one after another?

answers: Knowledge of the Lord and understanding to do good
easy.explanation: They have not known the Lord and have no knowledge of how to do good.

medium.explanation: The repeated cry expresses the prophet’s intense anguish.
medium.q: What feeling is expressed by “My bowels, my bowels!”?

answers: They are moved to another city
medium.explanation: He says, “Suddenly are my tents spoiled, and my curtains in a moment.”
medium.q: What happens to the prophet’s tents?

answers: A cry of grief and disaster
medium.explanation: “Woe” is a cry of sorrow in the face of ruin.

answers: The people chose evil and did not know how to do good
The prophet rejoiced in their wisdom
challenge.explanation: The passage links the coming destruction with a people skilled in evil but ignorant of goodness.
challenge.q: How is the prophet’s cry connected with the people’s lack of wisdom?

answers: That the ruin took many years
The speed and unexpectedness of the disaster
challenge.explanation: “Suddenly” and “in a moment” stress the abruptness of the ruin.
challenge.q: What does “suddenly are my tents spoiled” emphasize?

answers: In both places it signals war and danger
In both places it announces a celebration
It appears only in the earlier passage
challenge.explanation: The trumpet is associated with warning and the sound of war in both sections.
challenge.q: How is the trumpet in this passage related to the earlier war alarm?

paragraphs.title: The Vision of the Ruined Land and Incomplete Annihilation

easy.explanation: The prophet says the earth was “without form, and void.”
easy.q: How does the earth appear in the prophet’s vision?

easy.explanation: The vision says that the heavens had no light.
easy.q: What happens to the light of the heavens?

answers: It will last only one day
He will not make a full end
easy.explanation: Although the land will be desolate, the Lord says, “I will not make a full end.”
easy.q: What does the Lord emphasize about the desolation?

answers: A quiet sea and flourishing fields
medium.explanation: The mountains tremble and the hills move lightly.
medium.q: What natural events are described in the vision?

answers: Man and the birds of heaven
medium.explanation: The prophet sees no man, and the birds of heaven have fled.
medium.q: What is absent from the earth?

medium.explanation: The fruitful place becomes a wilderness, meaning it is ruined and deserted.
medium.q: What is a “wilderness” in this context?

answers: There will be severe ruin, but not total destruction
There will be no ruin at all
The land will remain full of cities
challenge.explanation: The land will be desolate, yet the Lord will not completely annihilate it.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between desolation and “I will not make a full end” teach?

answers: The presence and fierce anger of the Lord
challenge.explanation: The cities are broken down at the presence of the Lord and by his fierce anger.
challenge.q: What is given as the cause of the cities being broken down?

answers: The people remain to defend the city
Fear causes the people to abandon the cities
challenge.explanation: The people flee into thickets and rocks, and every city is forsaken.
challenge.q: What does the flight from the horsemen and bowmen show?

paragraphs.title: Israel as a Ravaged Woman and the Cry of Daughter Zion

easy.explanation: Israel is portrayed as spoiled and ravaged.
She clothes herself with crimson and decks herself with ornaments of gold.
easy.q: What does she try to do with crimson and gold ornaments?

answers: Like a woman in pain and in travail
easy.explanation: Her voice is compared with that of a woman in travail and one bringing forth her first child.
easy.q: How does Daughter Zion sound at the end?

answers: Her lovers despise her and seek her life
The city is too far away
medium.explanation: Her adornment is in vain because her lovers despise her and seek her life.
medium.q: Why does Israel’s adornment not help her?

answers: A woman bringing forth her first child
A lion coming from his thicket
medium.explanation: Her anguish is compared with that of a woman bringing forth her first child.
medium.q: What additional image describes Daughter Zion’s condition?

medium.explanation: To be spoiled here means to be plundered, ruined, and overcome.

answers: Outward appearance cannot save her from judgment
She is preparing for a feast
challenge.explanation: The passage says that making herself fair is in vain because destruction is coming.
challenge.q: What does the attempt to adorn herself reveal about Israel’s condition?

answers: Daughter Zion’s personal cry expresses the suffering caused by destruction and murder
The ending describes a successful harvest
challenge.explanation: Her anguish and cry of woe embody the suffering produced by the invading destruction.
challenge.q: How does the ending connect with the earlier description of war?

answers: Israel is helpless before the coming calamity
challenge.explanation: The question highlights Israel’s helplessness despite her attempts to adorn herself.
challenge.q: What does the question “what wilt thou do?” emphasize?
